notes.text: Hindi puts the verb last. Main chai pita hoon is literally I tea drink am. It stops feeling backwards fast.
Namaste and namaskar are the same bow, namaskar just sounds more formal. Friends skip both and say kya haal hai.
Aap, tum and tu all mean you. Choose wrong and you can insult or flirt by accident, so begin with aap.
Your father's brother is chacha, your mother's is mama. Hindi never says only uncle; which side of the family matters.
Roti, chapati and phulka are all flatbread, but a phulka has to puff up on the open flame. Puffing is the point.
Every number up to a hundred is its own word; 45 is paintalis. And people count in lakh and crore, not millions.
Gulabi, pink, just means rose-coloured, from gulab. English got orange from the same root as narangi, travelling through Persian.
Ask for the seedha rasta and you get the straight road. Seedha also means honest, or simple, depending on the sentence.
Kal means yesterday and tomorrow both. Only the verb tense tells you which, so listen right to the end.
Kitne ka hai is how much. Haggling is expected in a market, but never in a shop with printed price tags.
Tabiyat, borrowed from Arabic, means your nature or constitution. Meri tabiyat theek nahi is how you say I feel unwell.
Ghar is the home you live in, makaan is the building. A landlord rents out a makaan; you turn it into a ghar.
Kaam covers work, a task, and a favour. Mera ek kaam hai usually means I need something from you.
You can say main khush hoon, but for a feeling that just arrived Hindi prefers mujhe khushi hui: happiness happened to me.
Diwali comes from deepavali. Deep is lamp, avali is row: the festival is named after its own row of lights.
